# Operationalized implementation of the Phoenix Criteria

For version 1.x of the `phoenix` package, the provided functions focused on
applying the scoring rubric rowwise to a data set. As of version 2.0.0, new
functions apply the Phoenix criteria as they were developed in
[@Sanchez-Pinto2024](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.0196) and
[@Schlapbach2024](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.0179).

The scoring rubric is only part of the process of applying the Phoenix criteria.
That was the focus of this package for version 1.x. Here, we provide utilities
to use a patient's full electronic health record (EHR). Detailed guidance on
the process is provided in the online article [TODO: URL TO WEBSITE
ARTICLE](urlgoeshere) (and new publication? URL to go here).

For a concise introduction to both row-level scoring and this EHR workflow,
start with `vignette("quick-start", package = "phoenix")`.

The general workflow has four steps:

Unlike the direct `phoenix()` and `phoenix8()` wrappers, this workflow prepares
the antimicrobial and infectious-test inputs, establishes suspected infection,
and gates the Phoenix Sepsis Score and sepsis/septic-shock indicators on that
status.

0. Gather data.

1. Call `prepare_<input>()` functions to process each possible input
   for Phoenix or Phoenix-8 scoring.  These functions ensure the inputs are
   structured as needed for later processing and ensure that input values are
   within valid ranges. The default temporal tie-breakers, aggregations, and
   valid values and ranges are set to be consistent with @Sanchez-Pinto2024,
   but end users can modify them if desired.

2. Pass the outputs from step 1 into `prepare_phoenix_data()`. This function
   uses several default settings for look-back windows and other dynamic
   variables consistent with @Sanchez-Pinto2024, but end users can modify them
   if desired.

3. Pass the output from step 2 to `score_prepared_phoenix_data()`. This
   function uses defaults consistent with @Sanchez-Pinto2024 for observation
   windows, score thresholds, and aggregation methods. End users may modify
   those defaults as desired.

## Missingness, invalid input, and time alignment

Do not impute an unmeasured laboratory or vital-sign value. In this workflow,
last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) is not imputation: it carries an
actually observed, valid value forward in the time-indexed data only while it
remains within that input's look-back window. Once that window expires, the
criterion is unavailable and contributes zero points to the relevant scoring
component.

The `prepare_*()` functions validate observed rows. Raw missing values should
normally be represented by omitting the observation row, rather than by
including an `NA` value. Invalid, incorrectly scaled, or otherwise unusable
source values are data-quality problems: correct them when possible or exclude
them before preparation. They should not be treated as normal findings.

For example, an encounter with no lactate observation has no lactate row to
prepare. In contrast, a lactate recorded as `680` when the source unit was
mg/dL rather than mmol/L is an invalidly scaled observation. Convert it to the
expected unit or exclude it before calling `prepare_lactate()`; do not use it
as a missing or normal value.

## Example Data
```{r}
library(phoenix)
options(phoenix_verbose = TRUE)
```

The `phoenix` package comes with a synthetic data set `phx` used for this
example.  The data.frame is "long" data and has four columns:

1. `encounter_id`: a character string denoting `r length(unique(phx[["encounter_id"]]))`
   encounters. (Yes, these IDs look like dates; they are dates, but have nothing
   to do with any patient. They are the dates when the Colorado Avalanche won
   each of the first three Stanley Cups in franchise history.)
2. `encounter_clock`: the time, in minutes, from the start of the encounter to
   the reported observation, if applicable.
3. `variable`: a character string naming the reported variable.
4. `value`: the value of the `variable` at time `encounter_clock` for the
   `encounter_id`.
```{r, echo = TRUE, results = "markup"}
str(phx)
head(phx)
subset(phx, encounter_id == "19960610" & is.na(encounter_clock))
subset(phx, encounter_id == "19960610" & encounter_clock < 5)
```
For this data set we can see that the patient associated with `encounter_id`
19960610 is
`r subset(phx, encounter_id == "19960610" & variable == "age_months")[["value"]]`
months old, and within the first five minutes of the encounter, their
FiO<sub>2</sub> value was
`r paste0(100 * subset(phx, encounter_id == "19960610" & encounter_clock == 3 & variable == "fraction_of_inspired_oxygen")[["value"]], "%")`.

The variables in this data set are:
```{r}
sort(unique(phx[["variable"]]))
```

## Prepare Inputs

Each possible input for Phoenix-8 scoring has a corresponding
`prepare_<input>()` function. Calling each function ensures that its input is
structured as expected before scoring. For this section, we process variables
in the default order of the inputs to `prepare_phoenix_data()`: respiratory,
cardiovascular, neurologic, coagulation, endocrine, immunologic, renal, and
hepatic dysfunction.

All `prepare_<input>()` functions have several common arguments that end users
need to specify:

* `x`: a data.frame, or an object that inherits from a data.frame such as a
  data.table or tibble, containing one Phoenix input in long format.

* `id.vars`: a character vector of one or more column names in `x` that identify
  the encounter. Common examples are site, patient, and encounter identifiers.
  The same `id.vars`, in the same order, must be used for all inputs that will
  be combined with `prepare_phoenix_data`.

* `eclock`: a character vector of length one naming the encounter-clock column
  in `x`. The encounter clock is expected to be numeric, usually minutes from
  encounter start, with 0 denoting the start of the encounter. Age is static for
  the encounter and ignores `eclock`.

* `value.var`: a character vector of length one naming the column in `x` that
  contains the observed value for the Phoenix input being prepared.

Additional arguments can specify valid ranges and tie-breakers. Using the
defaults is consistent with the process used for @Sanchez-Pinto2024.

We will put the prepared inputs into a list for easier bookkeeping and later
use.
```{r}
prepared_inputs <- list()
```

### Respiratory Inputs

#### FiO<sub>2</sub>

The fraction of inspired oxygen is expected to be between 0.21 and 1.00.

```{r prepare-fio2}
prepared_inputs[["fio2"]] <-
  prepare_fio2(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "fraction_of_inspired_oxygen"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```
We received a message that duplicate rows were found and aggregated because
`options(phoenix_verbose = TRUE)` was set. Otherwise, messages are shown by
default in interactive sessions and suppressed in non-interactive sessions.

Let's look at a duplicated row:
```{r}
subset(
  x = phx,
  subset =
    variable == "fraction_of_inspired_oxygen" &
    encounter_clock == 10808 &
    encounter_id == 20220626
)

subset(
  x = prepared_inputs[["fio2"]],
  subset =
    encounter_clock == 10808 &
    encounter_id == 20220626
)
```
The default behavior is to take the maximum FiO<sub>2</sub> value when there are two
values at the same moment in time.

The fraction of inspired oxygen is expected to be between 0.21 and 1.00. If
your data contain a value such as 21, which is not uncommon in EHR data, an
error will be thrown:
```{r prepare-fio2-1, error = TRUE}
prepare_fio2(
  x = data.frame(patid = 1, eid = 2, t = 0, fio2 = 21),
  id.vars = c("patid", "eid"),
  eclock = "t",
  value.var = "fio2"
)
```

#### SpO<sub>2</sub>

The SpO<sub>2</sub> (pulse oximetry) is expected to be an integer value with a
maximum value of 100. The default valid range is any non-negative integer less than
100.  End users may find it useful to set a more restrictive lower bound.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["spo2"]] <-
  prepare_spo2(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "peripheral_capillary_oxygen_saturation"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

#### PaO<sub>2</sub>

The partial pressure of arterial oxygen is expected to be reported in units of
mmHg with non-negative values.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["pao2"]] <-
  prepare_pao2(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "partial_pressure_of_arterial_oxygen"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

#### Invasive Mechanical Ventilation
There are multiple possible inputs for invasive mechanical ventilation. One
option is an intubation indicator (0/1). If your data include that indicator,
you can call
`prepare_invasive_mechanical_ventilation_indicator()`.  No such variable is in
the `phx` data. Instead, there are several specific indicators of invasive
mechanical ventilation based on measurements of positive end-expiratory pressure
(PEEP) or mean airway pressure from a ventilator or high-frequency oscillatory ventilation
(HFOV).

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["mean_airway_pressure_ventilator"]] <-
  prepare_mean_airway_pressure_ventilator(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "mean_airway_pressure_ventilator"),
    id.vars = c("encounter_id"),
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["positive_end_expiratory_pressure"]] <-
  prepare_positive_end_expiratory_pressure(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "positive_end_expiratory_pressure"),
    id.vars = c("encounter_id"),
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )

# Two other functions but not with the phx data
# prepare_invasive_mechanical_ventilation_indicator()
# prepare_mean_airway_pressure_hfov()
```

#### O<sub>2</sub> Support

O<sub>2</sub> support is expected to be an indicator for any non-invasive oxygen
support.  In the `phx` data we have the `oxygen_flow` variable.  We will get an
error if passing that variable in directly to
`prepare_o2support()`.

```{r, error = TRUE}
prepare_o2support(
  x = subset(phx, variable == "oxygen_flow"),
  id.vars = c("encounter_id"),
  eclock = "encounter_clock",
  value.var = "value"
)
```

The reason for the error is that `oxygen_flow` is reported in liters per minute
and we simply need an indicator.

```{r}
head(subset(phx, variable == "oxygen_flow"))
o2 <- subset(phx, variable == "oxygen_flow")
o2[["value"]] <- as.integer(o2[["value"]] > 0)

prepared_inputs[["o2support"]] <-
  prepare_o2support(
    x = o2,
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Cardiovascular Inputs

Lactate, measured in mmol/L, is expected to be a non-negative floating point
value.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["lactate"]] <-
  prepare_lactate(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "lactate"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

Vasoactive medications are expected to be reported as indicators, 1 if the
patient is currently receiving a systemic vasoactive medication.  The dosage is
not considered here.   There are six medications of interest: dobutamine,
dopamine, epinephrine, milrinone, norepinephrine, and vasopressin.

For the example data set `phx`, only milrinone and epinephrine are reported.

```{r}
head(subset(phx, startsWith(variable, "systemic")))
prepared_inputs[["epinephrine"]] <-
  prepare_epinephrine(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "systemic_vasoactive_epinephrine"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["milrinone"]] <-
  prepare_milrinone(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "systemic_vasoactive_milrinone"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )

# Other prepare_<input>() functions for vasoactive medications
# prepare_dobutamine()
# prepare_dopamine()
# prepare_norepinephrine()
# prepare_vasopressin()
```

Mean arterial pressure can come directly from an arterial line or cuff, or it
can be estimated from systolic and diastolic pressures. All inputs here are
expected to be reported in mmHg.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["mean_arterial_pressure_arterial"]] <-
  prepare_mean_arterial_pressure_arterial(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "mean_arterial_pressure_arterial_line"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["mean_arterial_pressure_cuff"]] <-
  prepare_mean_arterial_pressure_cuff(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "mean_arterial_pressure_cuff"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )

prepared_inputs[["dbp_arterial"]] <-
  prepare_dbp_arterial(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "diastolic_blood_pressure_arterial_line"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["dbp_cuff"]] <-
  prepare_dbp_cuff(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "diastolic_blood_pressure_cuff"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )

prepared_inputs[["sbp_arterial"]] <-
  prepare_sbp_arterial(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "systolic_blood_pressure_arterial_line"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["sbp_cuff"]] <-
  prepare_sbp_cuff(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "systolic_blood_pressure_cuff"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

Lastly, the Phoenix score based on mean arterial pressure also depends on the
patient's age in months. There is no need to specify `eclock` when preparing
age because this example uses age at admission.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["age"]] <-
  prepare_age(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "age_months"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Neurological Inputs

The input for the neurologic organ dysfunction score is the total Glasgow Coma
Scale (GCS), which can be reported directly or calculated as the sum of the
three categories: eye, verbal, and motor. There is a non-trivial hierarchy for how
to assess the GCS over time.  We prepare the variables here and will let
`prepare_phoenix_data()` do the heavy lifting.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["gcseye"]] <-
  prepare_gcseye(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "glasgow_coma_scale_eye"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["gcsverbal"]] <-
  prepare_gcsverbal(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "glasgow_coma_scale_verbal"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["gcsmotor"]] <-
  prepare_gcsmotor(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "glasgow_coma_scale_motor"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["gcstotal"]] <-
  prepare_gcstotal(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "glasgow_coma_scale_total"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

An indicator for bilaterally fixed pupils is also used in the neurologic
assessment. We provide `prepare_pupils()` for bilateral fixation and separate
preparation methods for each eye. This supports longitudinal look-backs for
each eye when that level of information is available, without requiring end
users to construct the combined indicator.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["pupilleft"]] <-
  prepare_pupilleft(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "left_pupil_fixed"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["pupilright"]] <-
  prepare_pupilright(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "right_pupil_fixed"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )

# If you have an indicator for bilaterally fixed pupils use:
# prepare_pupils()
```

### Coagulation Inputs
The inputs for coagulation are platelets measured in 1000 / μL, INR (unitless),
DDimer in mg/L (FEU), and fibrinogen in mg/dL.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["platelets"]] <-
  prepare_platelets(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "platelets"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["inr"]] <-
  prepare_inr(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "international_normalized_ratio"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["ddimer"]] <-
  prepare_ddimer(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "fibrin_degradation_fragment"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["fibrinogen"]] <-
  prepare_fibrinogen(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "fibrinogen"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Endocrine Inputs
The endocrine system is only part of the Phoenix-8 scoring and can be ignored if
you are only interested in the four-system Phoenix score. The one input for
this system is glucose, measured in mg/dL.
```{r}
prepared_inputs[["glucose"]] <-
  prepare_glucose(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "glucose"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Immunologic Inputs
The immunologic system is only part of the Phoenix-8 scoring and can be ignored
if you are only interested in the four-system Phoenix score. The
absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) measured in 1000 cells / mm<sup>3</sup> and
absolute neutrophil count (ANC), also measured in 1000 cells / mm<sup>3</sup>,
are the two inputs.
```{r}
prepared_inputs[["alc"]] <-
  prepare_alc(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "absolute_lymphocyte_count"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["anc"]] <-
  prepare_anc(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "absolute_neutrophil_count"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Renal Inputs
The renal system is only part of the Phoenix-8 scoring and can be ignored if you
are only interested in the four-system Phoenix score.  The inputs for this
system are creatinine, measured in mg/dL, and age, measured in months. We only
need to prepare creatinine because age was already prepared in the cardiovascular
section.
```{r}
prepared_inputs[["creatinine"]] <-
  prepare_creatinine(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "creatinine"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Hepatic Inputs
The hepatic system is only part of the Phoenix-8 scoring and can be ignored if
you are only interested in the four-system Phoenix score.  There are two inputs
for this system, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) measured in IU / L, and total
bilirubin measured in mg/dL.
```{r}
prepared_inputs[["bilirubin"]] <-
  prepare_bilirubin(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "bilirubin"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["alt"]] <-
  prepare_alt(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "alanine_aminotransferase"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

### Suspected Infection
The Phoenix definition of sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction in the
presence of a suspected infection. Here we prepare the two inputs: an indicator
for the ordering of an infectious test and an indicator for a dose of a systemic
antimicrobial medication.

```{r}
prepared_inputs[["antimicrobials"]] <-
  prepare_antimicrobials(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "systemic_antimicrobial_medication"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
prepared_inputs[["antiinfectioustests"]] <-
  prepare_antiinfectioustests(
    x = subset(phx, variable == "infectious_test"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
```

## Prepare Phoenix Data
The `prepare_<input>()` methods prepare the data so that look-back windows and
relative hierarchies can be applied consistently. Each input
to `prepare_phoenix_data()` must be the return from the respective
`prepare_<input>()` function. By carefully selecting the names of the elements
in `prepared_inputs`, we can pass that list directly to
`prepare_phoenix_data()` via `do.call()`.

The result is a `data.frame` with the additional `prepared_phoenix_data` class,
which is used when scoring the data.

```{r, message = FALSE}
prepared_phoenix_data <-
  do.call(what = prepare_phoenix_data, args = prepared_inputs)
str(prepared_phoenix_data)
```

## Score the Prepared Phoenix Data

Score `prepared_phoenix_data` with a call to `score_prepared_phoenix_data()`.
This additional layer defines the observation window, score thresholds, and
aggregation method. By default, it uses the first 24 hours of the encounter,
expressed in minutes as $T = [T_0, T_1) = [0, 1440)$; a sepsis threshold of
$\sigma = 2$ points; a septic-shock cardiovascular threshold of $\kappa = 1$;
and the `jama2024` aggregation method.

```{r}
jama2024 <- score_prepared_phoenix_data(x = prepared_phoenix_data)
```

The result is a `data.frame` with one row per unique `id.vars` combination (in
this case, just `encounter_id`). The `suspected_infection` column is a 0/1
indicator for suspected infection within the observation window $T$.
The other columns use several terms and are of the form:

    <score>_<number-of-organ-systems>_<aggregation>

* `odss`: the organ dysfunction summary score
* `pss`: the Phoenix Sepsis Score, the product of the `suspected_infection`
  and `odss` columns
* number of organ systems: either 4 or 8
* aggregation: `jama2024` is the method consistent with @Sanchez-Pinto2024.
  The exploratory schemes are OLM (organ-level maximization), CCD
  (cardiovascular component decoupling), and FCD
  (full component decoupling).

In the preceding example, all three encounters had suspected infection. What if
that were not the case? Let's copy `prepared_inputs` and edit only the
antimicrobials. We will omit encounter 20220626 from the copy.

```{r, message = FALSE}
prepared_inputs_2 <- prepared_inputs
prepared_inputs_2[["antimicrobials"]] <-
  prepare_antimicrobials(
    x = subset(phx, encounter_id != "20220626" & variable == "systemic_antimicrobial_medication"),
    id.vars = "encounter_id",
    eclock = "encounter_clock",
    value.var = "value"
  )
jama2024_2 <-
  score_prepared_phoenix_data(x = do.call(prepare_phoenix_data, args = prepared_inputs_2))
jama2024_2
```

Notice that encounter 20220626 no longer has suspected infection. The
`odss_4_jama2024` column is still 5, but `pss_4_jama2024` is now 0, as is the
sepsis indicator. This is because ODSS is the organ dysfunction score without
considering infection status, whereas PSS and the sepsis flags account for
suspected infection status.

The Phoenix (`jama2024`) aggregation requires organ dysfunctions to be
concurrent in time. If we relax this requirement and sum the worst organ-system
scores over the observation window, we obtain the organ-level maximization
(OLM) aggregation.

```{r}
olm <-
  score_prepared_phoenix_data(x = prepared_phoenix_data, aggregation = "olm")
olm
```

Notice that in this output the column names use `olm` as a suffix.  Also,
encounter 19960610 has a higher score and is now classified as a case of sepsis
whereas under `jama2024` this encounter was not a case of sepsis.

The other aggregation methods can compound this effect.

```{r, message = FALSE}
ccd <-
  score_prepared_phoenix_data(x = prepared_phoenix_data, aggregation = "ccd")
ccd
```
```{r, message = FALSE}
fcd <-
  score_prepared_phoenix_data(x = prepared_phoenix_data, aggregation = "fcd")
fcd
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
plot_data <-
  rbind(
    with(jama2024, data.frame(encounter_id = encounter_id, y = odss_4_jama2024, aggregation = "jama2024")),
    with(olm, data.frame(encounter_id = encounter_id, y = odss_4_olm, aggregation = "olm")),
    with(ccd, data.frame(encounter_id = encounter_id, y = odss_4_ccd, aggregation = "ccd")),
    with(fcd, data.frame(encounter_id = encounter_id, y = odss_4_fcd, aggregation = "fcd"))
  )
plot_data[["aggregation"]] <-
  factor(plot_data[["aggregation"]], levels = c("jama2024", "olm", "ccd", "fcd"))

ggplot2::ggplot(data = plot_data) +
  ggplot2::aes(x = aggregation, y = y) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(w = 0.2)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(name = "", breaks = 0:10) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap( ~ encounter_id, nrow = 1L)
```
